The controller overstates dose because it assumes commissioning transmittance, while real transmittance and peak flow have cut the delivered dose
The flow meter under-reads in runoff
The sleeves foul only during runoff

inference.explanation: Transmittance and flow both moved against dose, the controller still assumes the old transmittance, and a bench calculation with real values reproduces the shortfall. Lamp, meter and sleeve options have no supporting checks.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the pacing error?

options.label: Archived controller configuration and seasonal transmittance records
Archived lamp output tests
Archived flow meter verification results

nextClue.explanation: Archived controller configuration and seasonal transmittance records directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Configuration shows the fixed commissioning value, and seasonal records show dose alarms beginning exactly when transmittance falls each spring.
clueText.nc-b: Lamp tests show full output in both seasons.
clueText.nc-c: Flow verification shows the meter accurate at high flow.

tasks.prompt: A chloraminated system in Saskatchewan is losing total chlorine residual in its storage tank, and nitrite has appeared in tank samples.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Tank nitrite measures 0.08 mg/L, up from below detection, and free ammonia in the tank has fallen.
Tank water age reaches nine days in a low demand period, and the tank temperature is at its summer high.
Alkalinity and pH in the tank have slipped slightly as nitrite rose.
Plant effluent entering the tank has a correct chlorine to ammonia ratio and a healthy total residual.
A neighbouring tank with faster turnover shows no nitrite and stable residual.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The plant is underdosing chlorine
Nitrification is establishing in the warm, high age tank, consuming chloramine and producing nitrite
The tank lining is consuming chlorine
Customers near the tank are using more water than metered

inference.explanation: Nitrite appears as free ammonia falls and alkalinity slips, the incoming water is correctly formed, and the faster turnover tank is unaffected. That is biological nitrification in the tank, not plant dosing, lining demand or customer use.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the nitrification pattern?

options.label: Archived tank nitrite, free ammonia and residual trends by season
Archived plant effluent ratio records
Archived tank lining inspection report

nextClue.explanation: Archived tank nitrite, free ammonia and residual trends by season directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Trends show nitrite episodes every warm high age period, resolving after turnover or boosting, and never in the fast turnover tank.
clueText.nc-b: Effluent ratio records are in target throughout the episodes.
clueText.nc-c: The lining inspection rated the coating sound.

tasks.prompt: A Manitoba plant raised its prechlorination dose to control algae at the intake, and treated water byproduct results climbed even though finished turbidity improved.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Raw dissolved organic carbon is high at 6.5 mg/L during the algae period.
Chlorine is applied ahead of coagulation, so it contacts the full raw organic load for hours.
A bench trial chlorinating after filtration, at the same final residual, formed about half the byproducts of the prechlorination trial.
Coagulation removes about half the organic carbon before the filters.
Final free residual and contact time are the same in both bench trials.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The laboratory byproduct results are contaminated
Applying chlorine before organics removal maximizes its contact with precursor material, and moving the point after filtration cuts formation
The algae themselves are a byproduct that the test detects
The chlorine product changed

inference.explanation: The bench trial changes only the point of application and halves formation at the same residual, while coagulation is shown removing half the precursors. Application point, not laboratory, algae or product causes, drives the result.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the application point effect?

options.label: Archived bench trial results by chlorination point with plant byproduct trends
Archived laboratory blank results
Archived chlorine delivery records

nextClue.explanation: Archived bench trial results by chlorination point with plant byproduct trends directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Trials and plant trends agree across two summers, with byproducts tracking prechlorination dose and organic load together.
clueText.nc-b: Laboratory blanks are clean in every batch.
clueText.nc-c: Deliveries show the same product through both summers.

tasks.prompt: Individual filter turbidity at a British Columbia plant runs at 0.7 NTU for hours after a coagulation upset, and the operator proposes relying on extra chlorine to cover the period.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Filtered turbidity at 0.7 NTU is well above the plant normal of under 0.1 NTU.
Particle counts in the effluent are about fifty times normal.
Bench disinfection tests in the plant manual show chlorine inactivation falling sharply in turbid water because organisms are shielded inside particles.
Chlorine residual and contact time are at their normal values.
Settled water quality recovers after the coagulation dose is corrected, and filter turbidity follows it down.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Extra chlorine fully compensates for any turbidity
Particles in the turbid effluent shield organisms from chlorine, so disinfection credit cannot be relied on until filtration recovers
The turbidity is only colour and carries no organisms
The contact tank will remove the particles given time

inference.explanation: Particle counts are fifty times normal, the manual documents shielding, and recovery tracks filtration, not chlorine changes. Turbidity here is particulate, the contact tank does not remove particles, and more chlorine does not reach shielded organisms.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the shielding concern?

options.label: Archived bench inactivation results at graded turbidity levels from the plant manual file
Archived chlorine dose log
Archived contact tank sludge survey

nextClue.explanation: Archived bench inactivation results at graded turbidity levels from the plant manual file directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The graded results show inactivation collapsing as turbidity rises past a few tenths, at constant residual and time.
clueText.nc-b: The dose log shows residual held normal through the upset, so chlorine was not the variable.
clueText.nc-c: The sludge survey is routine and unrelated to effluent particles.

tasks.prompt: A groundwater plant in Alberta disinfects in a contact pipeline, and its CT fell short after a well pump was replaced with a higher capacity unit.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: The new pump delivers 40 percent more flow than the old unit at the same setting.
Pipeline volume and chlorine residual are unchanged.
Tracer timing through the pipeline shortened in proportion to the flow increase.
Chlorine demand and temperature are at their usual values.
The CT sheet still uses the old pump flow from before the replacement.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The new pump damaged the pipeline lining, raising demand
Contact time fell in proportion to the higher flow, and the CT sheet still using the old flow hides the shortfall
The residual analyser was disturbed during the pump work
The well water changed when the pump was replaced

inference.explanation: Flow rose 40 percent, tracer time shortened in proportion, residual and demand are unchanged, and the sheet uses the old flow. The arithmetic of time and the stale sheet explain the shortfall without lining, analyser or source changes.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the flow change effect?

options.label: Archived pump test results and tracer timings before and after the replacement
Archived pipeline inspection report
Archived raw water quality comparison

nextClue.explanation: Archived pump test results and tracer timings before and after the replacement directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Tests confirm the capacity increase and tracer times shortened by the same proportion, dating the CT change to the swap.
clueText.nc-b: The inspection found the lining sound.
clueText.nc-c: Raw quality before and after is essentially identical.

tasks.prompt: Ozone dose at a Saskatchewan plant falls short on humid summer days, and the ozone residual in the contactor is low.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: The air preparation dryer dew point alarm activates on humid days, and feed gas dew point rises with it.
Ozone generator output measured at the unit falls as feed gas dew point rises, at constant power.
A test feeding dried air from a rental dryer restored generator output on a humid day.
Ozone demand of the water and contactor operation are steady.
Generator electrodes and power supply test within specification.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The water ozone demand rises in summer
Wet feed gas from the failing dryer cuts ozone generation, so dose falls on humid days
The generator is at the end of its life
The ozone residual analyser reads low in humidity

inference.explanation: Output tracks feed gas dew point, the dryer alarms, and dried air restores output on a humid day, while demand and generator hardware test normal. Feed gas moisture is the cause.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the dryer link?

options.label: Archived dew point and ozone output trends with dryer maintenance records
Archived ozone demand bench tests
Archived generator replacement assessments

nextClue.explanation: Archived dew point and ozone output trends with dryer maintenance records directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Trends show output sagging whenever dew point rises, and maintenance records show the dryer desiccant overdue for change.
clueText.nc-b: Demand tests are flat across the summer.
clueText.nc-c: Assessments rate the generator mid life and in specification.

tasks.prompt: A small plant in northern Manitoba found its clearwell free residual collapsing during spring turnover of its reservoir source, though the dose did not change.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Raw iron and manganese both spiked during turnover, to 1.9 mg/L and 0.4 mg/L.
Bench demand tests on turnover water show an immediate demand of 1.6 mg/L, against 0.4 mg/L on normal source water.
The plant dose of 1.2 mg/L was set from the normal demand tests.
Contact tank baffling and flow are unchanged.
After turnover passed, the same dose produced a normal residual again.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The chlorine feed degraded over the spring
Turnover demand from iron and manganese exceeds the set dose, leaving nothing for a free residual
The clearwell developed a short circuit in spring
The residual analyser fouls every spring

inference.explanation: Bench demand on turnover water exceeds the whole dose, the metals spiked, and the same dose recovered when turnover passed. Demand, not feed, hydraulics or the analyser, consumed the chlorine.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the turnover demand pattern?

options.label: Archived raw metals and bench demand results across past turnover events
Archived chlorine strength tests
Archived tracer study report

nextClue.explanation: Archived raw metals and bench demand results across past turnover events directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Each past turnover shows the same metals spike and demand jump, with residuals recovering as the lake settled.
clueText.nc-b: Strength tests show the product in specification each spring.
clueText.nc-c: The tracer report shows baffling at its design value.

tasks.prompt: Taste complaints and a swimming pool smell cluster in one pressure zone of a British Columbia town, while the rest of the system reports no problem.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: A booster chlorination station serves only the complaining zone, and its pump was replaced last week.
Free residual in the zone measures 1.9 mg/L against a system target near 0.6 mg/L, and residuals elsewhere are at target.
A drawdown test shows the new booster pump delivering about three times its set rate because its calibration was never checked.
Plant effluent residual and raw demand are normal.
Complaints began the day after the pump replacement.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The plant overdosed the whole system
The uncalibrated booster pump is overfeeding its zone, creating the high residual and the taste complaints there
A cross connection is adding pool water to the zone
The zone has developed a contamination problem

inference.explanation: Only the booster zone is affected, its pump delivers triple its setting after an unchecked replacement, and complaints date to the swap. Plant wide overdose and cross connection or contamination causes contradict the normal results elsewhere.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the booster error?

options.label: Archived booster station drawdown and residual records around the pump change
Archived plant effluent residual log
Archived cross connection survey for the zone

nextClue.explanation: Archived booster station drawdown and residual records around the pump change directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Records show zone residuals stepping up the day of the swap and drawdown confirming triple delivery, while plant effluent stayed at target.
clueText.nc-b: Plant effluent residuals are flat and at target throughout.
clueText.nc-c: The zone survey found no unprotected cross connections.

tasks.prompt: A Saskatchewan plant on chloramines sees total residual hold well but receives complaints of weak disinfection protection after a source ammonia change.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Raw ammonia fell to near zero after a source switch, and the plant stopped its ammonia feed believing the source still supplied enough.
Speciation shows most of the residual is now free chlorine rather than monochloramine, reversing the intended form.
Total chlorine residual reads at target, masking the speciation change.
Bench tests adding the former ammonia dose restore monochloramine as the dominant species.
Chlorine feed and contact time are unchanged.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Total residual is at target so nothing has changed
Without the ammonia feed the plant is no longer forming chloramine, and the total residual figure hides the change in species
The source switch introduced a chlorine demand
The speciation test is unreliable

inference.explanation: Speciation shows free chlorine dominant after the ammonia feed stopped, total residual masks it, and bench ammonia addition restores monochloramine. The strategy changed in fact, whatever the total figure suggests.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the speciation shift?

options.label: Archived chlorine speciation results before and after the source switch
Archived total residual log
Archived chlorine demand tests

nextClue.explanation: Archived chlorine speciation results before and after the source switch directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Speciation records show monochloramine dominant for years and free chlorine dominant from the switch onward.
clueText.nc-b: The total log is flat, which is exactly why the change was missed.
clueText.nc-c: Demand tests are unchanged across the switch.

tasks.prompt: During a January cold snap at a Yukon plant, virus inactivation credit fell short even though Giardia style CT checks on the sheet looked acceptable.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Water temperature is 0.5 C, the coldest the plant records.
The plant manual CT tables show virus inactivation needs much more CT at near zero temperature than the values the sheet used, which came from a 10 C table.
Residual, pH and T10 are measured correctly and are at normal values.
Recalculating with the near zero temperature virus table shows the shortfall plainly.
No feed, baffle or flow changes occurred during the snap.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The sheet used the wrong temperature table, understating the CT that virus inactivation needs in near freezing water
The chlorine feed failed in the cold
The contact tank iced over and short-circuited
The residual analyser reads falsely at low temperature

inference.explanation: Inputs are verified correct and only the table temperature was wrong, with recalculation exposing the shortfall. Feed, ice and analyser causes have no supporting observation during the snap.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the table error?

options.label: Archived CT sheets with the manual temperature tables for past winters
Archived chlorine feed log
Archived contact tank inspection record

nextClue.explanation: Archived CT sheets with the manual temperature tables for past winters directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Past winter sheets show the same 10 C table used every year and shortfalls appearing whenever the correct table is applied to cold snaps.
clueText.nc-b: The feed log shows steady delivery through the snap.
clueText.nc-c: Inspection found the tank free of ice blockage.

tasks.prompt: A Manitoba plant wants to cut chlorine dose because finished water tastes of chlorine, but the operator suspects the real problem sits in the clearwell.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Clearwell baffling was downgraded after a tracer study to a factor of 0.3, so the plant holds a high residual to compensate for poor contact time efficiency.
A sister plant with baffling near 0.7 meets its CT at about half the residual.
Chlorine demand of the treated water is low and similar at both plants.
Taste complaints track the high plant residual, not any distribution booster.
A baffle repair design in the plant files would restore the factor to about 0.7.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The treated water demand forces the high residual
Poor baffling forces the plant to buy its CT with residual instead of time, and fixing the baffles is the route to a lower dose
The chlorine product is unusually strong tasting
Customers are unusually sensitive in this town

inference.explanation: Demand is low and matches the sister plant, which earns the same CT at half the residual with good baffling. The clearwell hydraulics, documented by tracer, are what the high residual compensates for.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the baffling comparison?

options.label: Archived tracer studies and CT sheets for both plants
Archived chlorine demand bench results
Archived taste complaint surveys

nextClue.explanation: Archived tracer studies and CT sheets for both plants directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The studies and sheets show identical demand and time, with residual needs differing in proportion to the baffling factors.
clueText.nc-b: Demand results are low and equal at both plants.
clueText.nc-c: Surveys show complaints tracking residual levels, not neighbourhoods.

tasks.prompt: After a wildfire in its watershed, a British Columbia plant finds chlorine demand and byproduct formation both elevated for months.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Raw dissolved organic carbon measures 9.2 mg/L, about triple the pre fire value, with ash and charred debris visible at the intake.
Bench demand tests track the organic carbon, rising and falling together.
Enhanced coagulation jar tests remove much of the extra organic carbon and cut bench byproduct formation by about half.
Plant hydraulics, feed equipment and chlorine product all test normal.
Turbidity is only moderately elevated and settles well.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The chlorine product was contaminated during the fire response
Fire driven organic loading in the source is raising demand and byproduct formation, and enhanced coagulation is the control point
The filters are damaged by ash
A new industrial discharge began after the fire

inference.explanation: Organic carbon tripled, demand tracks it, and jars removing it cut byproduct formation, while equipment and product test normal. Source organics from the burn explain both symptoms together.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the fire loading pattern?

options.label: Archived raw organic carbon and demand results before and after the fire
Archived chlorine supplier records
Archived filter inspection report

nextClue.explanation: Archived raw organic carbon and demand results before and after the fire directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The record shows both measures stepping up with the first runoff after the fire and easing slowly together over months.
clueText.nc-b: Supplier records show the same product as before the fire.
clueText.nc-c: The filter inspection found ash fouling cleaned at the first backwash.

tasks.prompt: A plant in Alberta reports good CT on paper during a week when its contact tank was half drained for inspection prep, and the reviewer questions the claim.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Tank level records show the contact tank at half its normal depth for five days.
The CT sheets for those days use the full tank volume in the time calculation.
Flow and residual were at normal values.
A tracer test done at half depth last year gave a T10 about half the full depth value.
The inspection itself found the baffles in good order.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The reviewer is mistaken and the CT was fine
The claimed CT is overstated because the half depth tank held about half the contact time the sheets assumed
The residual must have doubled to compensate
The flow meter over-read during the inspection week

inference.explanation: Level records and the sheets disagree on volume, and a prior half depth tracer confirms the time halved, at normal flow and residual. The claim rests on a volume the tank did not hold that week.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the half depth effect?

options.label: Archived tank level records with the half depth tracer result
Archived residual log
Archived flow meter verification

nextClue.explanation: Archived tank level records with the half depth tracer result directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Levels confirm five half depth days and the tracer shows T10 halving at that depth, matching the sheets full volume error.
clueText.nc-b: The residual log shows normal values, with no compensating rise.
clueText.nc-c: Flow verification shows the meter accurate that month.

tasks.prompt: A dual media filter at an Alberta plant loses its anthracite cap unevenly, and one side of the bed has gone mostly to sand at the surface.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: A level survey shows the backwash trough on the low side sitting 4 cm lower than the trough on the high side.
Anthracite depth is much thinner above the low trough and near normal elsewhere.
Backwash expansion and total flow are at target for the whole filter.
Media samples show the anthracite itself is sound and correctly sized.
The trough level difference dates from a trough repair last year.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The anthracite is dissolving on one side
The low trough spills wash water and media preferentially on its side, stripping the cap there at a normal total backwash rate
The sand is migrating upward on one side
Operators are skimming the bed unevenly

inference.explanation: Total backwash rate is at target, the media is sound, and the loss maps exactly to the side with the low trough left by the repair. Preferential spilling over the low trough explains a one sided loss that product, migration and skimming options cannot.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the trough effect?

options.label: Archived trough level surveys and media depth surveys by side
Archived media product certificates
Archived operator round sheets

nextClue.explanation: Archived trough level surveys and media depth surveys by side directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Surveys show the level gap appearing after the repair and the anthracite thinning only on that side at each survey since.
clueText.nc-b: Certificates show standard media that performed evenly for years.
clueText.nc-c: Round sheets show no manual skimming of the bed surface.
